strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: dependence on rare, sensitive, and costly real abnormal footage. The idea of replacing real abnormal videos with class-aware diffusion-generated pseudo anomalies is timely and potentially useful for deployment.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: CLIP-based normal-frame retrieval anchors image-to-video generation to plausible surveillance scenes, VLM prompt refinement improves generated-video consistency, and DARM attempts to compensate for pseudo-video feature bias when training a UR-DMU-style detector.

Empirical results are promising, especially on ShanghaiTech, where PA-VAD reports 98.2% frame-level AUC while using no real abnormal training videos, and the ablations suggest that prompt refinement and the usage-aware memory update contribute meaningfully.

The paper includes useful qualitative examples, generation-quality metrics, a study on the number of synthesized clips, hyperparameters, and computational-cost reporting, which improves transparency compared with many generation-based papers.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol is not fully convincing relative to the strength of the claims. The method uses abnormal class names to synthesize training data, yet it is repeatedly compared to UVAD methods as operating under the same constraint. This is a materially different setting from normal-only UVAD, and the paper should frame it as class-informed pseudo-supervision rather than broadly as unsupervised or fully comparable to UVAD.

The most relevant comparison to other pseudo-anomaly or generation-based VAD methods is weak. GV-VAD and spatio-temporal pseudo-anomaly generation are discussed, but no quantitative comparison is provided under matched conditions. This makes it difficult to isolate whether the gains come from the proposed CA-PAG/DARM design or simply from using a stronger modern video generator and a strong UR-DMU backbone.

Evidence for DARM's central motivation is thin. The claimed MIL bias from inflated pseudo-video magnitudes is supported mainly by one mean feature-norm table on UCF-Crime, and DARM aligns real normal with pseudo-normal features rather than directly addressing the unavailable real abnormal distribution. More diagnostics, per-class analysis, score-distribution analysis, and UCF-Crime ablations would be needed to substantiate the mechanism.

The reported superiority over real-abnormal WVAD is limited and somewhat overstated. The method surpasses WVAD baselines on ShanghaiTech by a small margin but remains below strong real-abnormal methods on UCF-Crime by several AUC points. Since UCF-Crime is the larger and more challenging benchmark, the conclusion that pseudo-only training can match or exceed Real/Real pipelines is only partially supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The exact prompt sets, full VLM instruction, generation filtering policy, pseudo-normal generation procedure, and code/data release plan are not sufficiently specified in the main paper. Because the method depends heavily on proprietary-scale models and prompt details, small implementation differences could materially affect results.

The evaluation is narrow: only two datasets, no cross-dataset generalization, no robustness to unseen abnormal classes, no analysis of failure cases beyond a small qualitative example, and no repeated runs or confidence intervals. This is a concern because generated pseudo data may overfit benchmark category names and scene priors.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: the paper alternates between calling the setup weakly supervised and unsupervised; Table 5 is hard to parse because some rows omit CA-PAG components while adding DARM components; and some grammatical/formatting errors suggest the method details would benefit from tightening.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: the scarcity, cost, and privacy sensitivity of real abnormal footage. Training without real abnormal videos is a meaningful goal for deployment-oriented VAD.

The overall framework is plausible and coherent: CLIP-based seed-image selection, VLM prompt refinement, image-to-video generation, and a regularized detector are sensible components for building pseudo-abnormal supervision.

The paper reports strong headline results, especially on ShanghaiTech, where the proposed method reaches 98.2% AUC and appears competitive even with methods trained on real abnormal videos. The ablations suggest that prompt refinement and the DARM module both contribute.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, including generator choice, resolution, frame count, guidance scales, training hyperparameters, and generation cost. The authors also acknowledge generation failures for subtle/context-heavy crimes such as shoplifting.
weaknesses: I assess this primarily as an Algorithms/General paper, though it also has an Applied/Systems flavor. Under either framing, the experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. The central claim that pseudo anomalies can replace real abnormal data is supported mainly by two datasets and AUC tables, without enough controls to isolate whether gains come from generation, dataset-specific class priors, backbone choices, or protocol advantages.

The comparison protocol is problematic. The method uses abnormal class names and generates class-conditioned abnormal videos, while UVAD baselines do not use abnormal-class metadata; calling that comparison fully fair is overstated. Comparisons to WVAD methods are also not apples-to-apples because those methods train with real abnormal videos but may not use the same backbone, feature extractor, augmentations, or tuning budget.

The paper does not sufficiently rule out dataset/protocol leakage or overfitting to benchmark labels. It uses known abnormal class names from the benchmark to synthesize training data, then evaluates on the same benchmark classes. This may be valid as a specific open-set/closed-class setting, but the paper presents it as broadly reducing anomaly-data collection costs without testing transfer to unseen anomaly categories, new scenes, or new datasets.

The empirical validation of generated video quality is weak. FID/KID/FVD/KVD are reported only in a small table for SHT, with no clear sample sizes, no confidence intervals, and no evidence that these metrics correlate with downstream anomaly detection. The qualitative examples are limited, and the supplementary failure case suggests that some classes may not contain clear abnormal cues.

The DARM motivation is underdeveloped. The claimed issue is inflated feature magnitude in pseudo anomalies, but the only evidence is a mean norm comparison of 20.52 vs. 23.03 on UCF-Crime. There is no distributional analysis, no statistical test, and no direct demonstration that the proposed losses specifically solve magnitude-driven MIL bias rather than acting as generic regularizers.

Several methodological details are unclear or inconsistent. The main paper defines negative CLIP scoring with s_neg but does not clearly specify aggregation over multiple negative phrases. Pseudo-normal generation is used for domain alignment but is not described with the same rigor as pseudo-abnormal generation. The ablation table formatting is hard to interpret, and some rows appear redundant or ambiguous after extraction.

The paper omits important baselines and controls. It should compare against simpler pseudo-anomaly generation strategies, random seed image selection, raw class prompts, text-to-video generation, synthetic data without DARM, DARM on real abnormal training, and modern VLM/VAD baselines under matched features. The cited closest generation-based method GV-VAD is discussed but not quantitatively compared.

The results lack robustness reporting. There are no standard deviations across random seeds, no sensitivity analysis for CLIP Top-K, prompt templates, generator choice, number of pseudo-normal clips, or DARM hyperparameters beyond the number of pseudo-abnormal clips on SHT. Given the heavy use of large generative and vision-language models, reproducibility and variance are serious concerns.

The writing sometimes overclaims. Statements such as 'Pseudo Anomalies Are All You Need' and 'fully fair' UVAD comparison are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially since UCF-Crime remains below real-abnormal WVAD methods and the method relies on benchmark abnormal class names and expensive generation with a large video diffusion model.

The societal and deployment discussion is thin. A system that synthesizes surveillance anomalies and trains detectors for public-safety settings raises questions about bias, false alarms, privacy, misuse, and whether generated anomalies amplify generator priors; these are not meaningfully analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: the scarcity, privacy sensitivity, and collection cost of real abnormal videos. The proposed pseudo-only training setting is meaningful, and the claim is clearly positioned against both UVAD and WVAD protocols.

The overall framework is well motivated and technically coherent. CA-PAG uses class-aware CLIP retrieval and VLM prompt refinement to make image-to-video generation more scene-consistent, while DARM addresses a plausible failure mode of generated videos, namely inflated motion/feature magnitude bias in MIL training.

The empirical results are strong for the claimed setting. PA-VAD reaches 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime without real abnormal training videos, outperforming UVAD baselines and even surpassing reported real-abnormal WVAD methods on ShanghaiTech.

The ablations support the design: prompt refinement improves CA-PAG, DARM improves over the UR-DMU backbone in the same Real/Pseudo setting, and the usage-aware update plus domain alignment gives the best result. The analysis of synthetic data quantity and the qualitative examples also help substantiate the method.

The paper is mostly clear and includes useful implementation details in the supplement, including generator choice, resolution, frame count, hyperparameters, and generation cost. The stated limitation on long-horizon/context-heavy UCF-Crime anomalies is appropriate and strengthens the framing.
weaknesses: The comparison protocol is somewhat delicate. The method uses abnormal class names at training/generation time, which gives it semantic prior information unavailable to standard UVAD methods. Calling the UVAD comparison fully fair is therefore too strong; the setting is better described as class-name-supervised or generation-assisted anomaly detection rather than pure normal-only UVAD.

The originality is moderate rather than high. Much of the pipeline builds from strong off-the-shelf components: CLIP retrieval, VLM prompt rewriting, Wan2.2 generation, and UR-DMU. DARM is useful, but the domain-adversarial and prototype-usage ideas are incremental combinations rather than a fundamentally new detection formulation.

The evidence is strong but still narrow. Only two datasets are evaluated, and the most convincing win over real-abnormal WVAD is on ShanghaiTech; on UCF-Crime the method remains below several Real/Real WVAD baselines. Broader evaluation on additional surveillance datasets or cross-dataset transfer would make the deployment claim more convincing.

Some methodological details need tightening for reproducibility and interpretation. The paper does not fully specify how pseudo-normal clips are generated, how many seeds/runs are used, whether results have variance, or whether synthetic clip selection/failure filtering is performed beyond the described process.

The generation-quality evaluation is limited. FVD/FID/KVD/KID are reported mainly for prompt refinement and do not directly validate whether the synthesized clips contain correct anomalous semantics. Human evaluation or automated anomaly-label consistency checks would better support the central pseudo-anomaly supervision claim.

There are minor clarity and polish issues, including grammar errors, duplicated/near-duplicated overview figures, and an occasional mismatch in terminology between unsupervised, weakly supervised, Real/Pseudo, and class-aware generation settings. These do not undermine the main contribution but should be cleaned up.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem in video anomaly detection: reducing reliance on real abnormal footage, which is often scarce, sensitive, or costly to collect.
The pseudo-only framing is clear and potentially impactful, especially for surveillance settings where normal footage and anomaly class names may be available but real abnormal examples are not.
The method combines a plausible generation pipeline, CA-PAG, with CLIP-based seed selection and VLM prompt refinement, plus DARM to mitigate the observed feature-magnitude bias from generated videos.

Experiments cover three common VAD benchmarks, with strong reported AUCs: 98.2 on ShanghaiTech, 82.5 on UCF-Crime, and 95.1 on XD-Violence. The gains over the authors' pseudo-only UR-DMU baseline are consistent across datasets.

The ablations are useful: initial-image selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware memory updates are separately evaluated; the number-of-generated-clips study and open-set experiments add supporting evidence.
The paper includes meaningful limitations, especially the difficulty of synthesizing long, context-heavy anomalies on UCF-Crime, and reports generation cost in the supplement.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not fully controlled. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, while several WVAD baselines use I3D or C3D; improvements over Real/Real methods may partly come from stronger pretrained features rather than the pseudo-only training strategy or DARM.

The supervision setting is somewhat between UVAD and WVAD: the method uses abnormal class names, CLIP/VLM priors, and a large video diffusion model. The paper acknowledges this, but some claims against UVAD and Real/Real WVAD baselines still read stronger than the evidence supports.

There is no same-backbone Real/Real upper-bound comparison for the proposed detector. A Qwen2.5-VL + UR-DMU/DARM model trained with real abnormal videos would clarify whether pseudo-only training is genuinely competitive or just benefits from feature/backbone changes.

Comparison to prior pseudo-generation methods is limited and mostly quoted from papers rather than rerun under matched features, generators, datasets, and protocols. This weakens conclusions about the novelty and effectiveness of CA-PAG relative to existing pseudo-anomaly generation.

The generation-quality evaluation is thin: Table 3 reports metrics only for SHT and only compares prompt refinement variants. More dataset-wide evaluation, human verification, or anomaly-class fidelity analysis would strengthen the claim that generated videos provide meaningful abnormal supervision rather than artifacts.

Some implementation details remain under-specified for reproducibility, including exact prompt templates, pseudo-normal generation procedure, sampling/selection details, and how many generated clips are retained or filtered after failures.

The DARM explanation is plausible but not fully theoretically grounded. Domain alignment is applied to normal/pseudo-normal streams, while the most important correction appears to occur in abnormal memory usage; the causal link between these losses and real-anomaly generalization needs stronger evidence.

The reported detector-space norm analysis uses real abnormal features for diagnosis, but the paper should be clearer that these are not used for training and should discuss whether hyperparameters or design decisions were tuned using such test-side observations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing dependence on scarce, sensitive real abnormal surveillance footage for video anomaly detection.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually appealing: selecting normal seed frames with CLIP, refining anomaly prompts with a VLM, synthesizing image-to-video pseudo anomalies, and then regularizing a MIL detector against pseudo-domain shortcuts.

The manuscript includes useful ablations over seed selection, prompt refinement, DARM components, number of synthesized clips, and an open-set-style evaluation. The explicit discussion of pseudo-generation failures and UCF-Crime limitations is appreciated.
weaknesses: The central experimental claim is not convincingly supported because comparisons mix protocols, features, and supervision. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features and large pretrained VLM/diffusion priors, while many baselines use I3D/C3D or no frozen clip backbone, and most prior numbers are quoted rather than reproduced under a common feature/backbone. This makes the reported gains over UVAD/WVAD baselines hard to attribute to the proposed method.

The supervision setting is overstated. The method uses target abnormal class names, apparently including benchmark anomaly categories, to synthesize training clips. This is not normal-only unsupervised VAD in the usual sense, and it weakens comparisons to UVAD methods that do not receive the test anomaly taxonomy. The paper should frame this as class-name-supervised pseudo-anomaly training, not simply abnormal-free or unsupervised.

The novelty of DARM is limited and insufficiently isolated. Domain-adversarial alignment and memory/prototype usage regularization are standard ingredients, and the paper builds directly on UR-DMU. The evidence that these components specifically solve a newly identified “spatiotemporal magnitude bias” is not fully convincing; the strongest norm evidence is in the trained detector space, where DARM directly changes the representation and memory dynamics, so it risks being partly circular.

Several important implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility: exact generated prompts, VLM instructions, pseudo-normal generation procedure, frame sampling from normal videos, train/validation selection, random seeds/splits, and whether generated videos or code will be released. The supplementary material says the full Chinese VLM prompt is provided, but the extracted text only gives a simplified example.

The evaluation may involve target-dataset or target-class tuning that is not carefully controlled. Hyperparameters, clip counts, guidance scales, and generated categories are dataset-specific, and there is no validation protocol explaining how these were chosen without using abnormal validation signals.

The generation-quality evaluation is weakly connected to detection utility. FID/FVD/KID/KVD are reported for only a small comparison, with unclear reference distributions and no statistical uncertainty. The paper also acknowledges that some classes generate vague or missing abnormal cues, but does not quantify per-class generation success or its impact on detection.

The open-set results are promising but not enough to resolve the supervision concern: even the “seen class” protocol still relies on abnormal class names and powerful pretrained generative priors, and comparisons to OpenVAD/RTFM are again not controlled for backbone and training setup.

Claims such as surpassing real-abnormal WVAD baselines on ShanghaiTech and XD-Violence are too strong given the uncontrolled backbone/pretraining differences, small margins, and different data protocols. On UCF-Crime, the method remains well below real-abnormal WVAD and single-frame-supervised methods despite substantial external pretrained knowledge and generation cost.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically motivated VAD setting: training without any real abnormal videos. This is a meaningful contribution because real abnormal surveillance footage is scarce, privacy-sensitive, and costly, and the paper makes a convincing case that pseudo-only training can be competitive when paired with suitable regularization.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and well targeted to the problem. CLIP-based scene/class-relevant seed selection, VLM prompt refinement, and image-to-video diffusion form a plausible pseudo-anomaly generator, while DARM directly addresses the observed feature-magnitude bias induced by synthesized clips.

The experimental evidence is relatively strong across three standard benchmarks. PA-VAD obtains 98.2 AUC on ShanghaiTech, 82.5 on UCF-Crime, and 95.1 on XD-Violence, outperforming UVAD baselines and even surpassing some real-abnormal WVAD baselines on ShanghaiTech and XD-Violence.

The ablations are useful and support the technical claims: CLIP initial-image selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware updates each contribute, and the feature-norm analysis provides a concrete mechanism explaining why naive pseudo-anomaly training fails.

The open-set experiments are a notable strength. The method improves over OpenVAD under restricted seen-class settings, suggesting that the model is not merely memorizing generated class artifacts and that DARM helps transfer to unseen anomalies.

The paper is generally clear, includes implementation details and hyperparameters in the supplement, and acknowledges a real limitation on UCF-Crime where long-horizon, context-heavy anomalies remain difficult to synthesize.
weaknesses: The contribution is strongest as an applied/algorithmic VAD framework rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm. CA-PAG combines existing pretrained components, and DARM builds on UR-DMU with domain-adversarial alignment and a memory-balancing loss. This is still valuable, but the novelty is more in the problem formulation and integration than in entirely new modeling primitives.

Comparisons are somewhat complicated by unequal pretrained knowledge and feature backbones. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, Qwen3 VLM prompt refinement, CLIP retrieval, and Wan2.2 generation, whereas several baselines use older I3D/C3D or different supervision. The paper notes this, but stronger controlled comparisons with the same feature extractor and backbone would make the gains easier to attribute.

The pseudo-video generation quality evaluation is limited. FVD/FID/KVD/KID are reported only briefly, apparently on ShanghaiTech, and there is no human or task-specific validation of whether generated clips truly express the intended abnormal classes. This matters because the detector may benefit from artifacts or broad motion cues rather than semantically faithful anomalies.

The method depends on large pretrained generative and vision-language models and substantial generation cost: tens of hours on two RTX 6000 Ada GPUs for full pseudo sets. This is acceptable for offline training, but it weakens claims of broad practicality unless code, generated data, prompts, and reproducibility details are released.

The strongest WVAD methods on UCF-Crime remain clearly ahead, and Table 7 shows a sizable gap to SF-VAD/FPL and generation-plus-real-abnormal methods on Crime. The paper explains this via long-horizon anomalies, but this also indicates that the pseudo-only setting is not yet a general replacement for real abnormal videos.

Some evaluation choices need more scrutiny. Prior numbers are mostly quoted from papers rather than rerun, statistical variation is reported only for the open-set experiments, and the main benchmark results lack confidence intervals or multiple-seed analysis. Given the small number of generated clips in some settings, variance could be nontrivial.

Reproducibility is partially but not fully addressed. Hyperparameters and generation settings are provided, but exact prompts, seed selection details, generated clip lists, and whether generated pseudo data will be released are critical for reproducing this type of method.
